title: Radio & Records
cardDescription: Records, radio controls, and familiar ways to listen at home.
description: Settle in with a crossword about records, radios, and the familiar parts that bring recorded music into a room.
focus: This puzzle follows the listening equipment rather than asking you to name performers or remember song titles. The answers cover record materials, player parts, and everyday controls. Clues distinguish an object from the sound or recording it carries.
solvingTip: Picture which part you would touch: a dial, a sleeve, or the volume control. A clue about the material of a record calls for a different answer from a clue about its spiral track. Crossing letters can help with the longer equipment names.
words: Receiver used to listen to broadcast stations
A grooved disc played on a turntable
Plastic material used to make many phonograph records
A collection of recorded songs released together
Rotating platform on which a phonograph record rests
Common name for the stylus that follows a record's groove
Spiral track on a record that a stylus follows
Part of a radio used to select a station
Round control or scale used to tune many older radios
Small projecting control turned by hand
Device that turns an audio signal into sound you can hear
Control setting that makes recorded sound louder or softer
Protective paper or cardboard covering for a record
Small case containing magnetic tape for recorded sound
Long magnetic strip used to record sound
One playing surface of a record, labeled A or B
Sound reproduction with separate left and right channels
Short form of monophonic, describing single-channel sound
Rod or wire used to receive radio signals
Pivoting arm that carries a record player's cartridge

answerNotes.VINYL: Vinyl names a material, not every kind of record ever made. Many earlier 78 rpm records were made from shellac-based compounds, so the clue says 'many' rather than 'all.'
answerNotes.NEEDLE: Needle is the familiar name for a record player's stylus. It follows the groove, while the tonearm holds the cartridge assembly above the rotating record.
answerNotes.GROOVE: The groove is the physical path traced by the stylus. A song or track is the recorded content; the clue is asking for the path on the disc.
answerNotes.MONO: Mono sound uses one channel. Stereo separates left and right channels; the distinction concerns the recording and playback signal, not simply how many speaker boxes you can see.
answerNotes.SLEEVE: A sleeve protects the record itself. Album can describe the collection of recorded music, so the object named in the clue matters.
answerNotes.TURNTABLE: Turntable names the rotating platform, and is also used for a complete record-playing unit. The clue uses the platform meaning to make the answer precise.

title: At the Piano
cardDescription: Keyboard parts, simple musical patterns, and playing at the piano.
description: Explore a piano's keys, pedals, and everyday musical patterns in a relaxed puzzle that needs no music-reading experience.
focus: The clues stay close to the keyboard: what the player touches, what is inside an acoustic piano, and a few familiar patterns of notes. No printed notation or performance is required. When a clue describes a mechanical part, it refers to an acoustic piano rather than every digital keyboard.
solvingTip: Separate the object from the action it produces. A key is pressed by a finger, while a hammer strikes a string inside an acoustic piano. A clue about several notes together points to a pattern rather than a single piano part.
words: Keyboard instrument whose name can also mean soft in musical directions
One of the black or white levers a pianist presses
Foot-operated lever below a piano keyboard
Taut wire struck to make sound in an acoustic piano
Felt-covered part that strikes a piano string
Seat often used by a pianist
Hinged top cover of a grand piano
Written music showing the notes to be played
A piece of printed music is often called ___ music
Interval from one C to the next C above or below it
Group of musical notes sounded together
Sequence of notes arranged in ascending or descending pitch
A single musical tone or the written symbol for it
A period of silence indicated in written music
Body part whose fingers press the piano keys
One of the digits used to press a piano key
A melody you might pick out on a piano
Color of the wider, lower row of piano keys
Color of the raised keys arranged in groups of two and three
Two performers playing together, such as a piano ___

answerNotes.HAMMER: In an acoustic piano, pressing a key sets a hammer in motion toward the strings. The finger does not strike the strings directly, which distinguishes the key from the hammer.
answerNotes.PEDAL: Piano pedals have different jobs. The familiar sustain pedal lets notes continue after the keys are released; the clue asks for the foot-operated part without assuming all pedals work alike.
answerNotes.OCTAVE: Moving from one C to the next C reaches an octave. The interval can begin on any note; C is used as a familiar example rather than as a special requirement.
answerNotes.CHORD: A chord brings notes together, while a scale arranges notes in a sequence. The words 'together' and 'ascending or descending' help distinguish the clues.
answerNotes.BLACK: The raised black keys repeat in groups of two and three. This pattern helps a pianist locate notes without needing the keys to be labeled.
answerNotes.REST: A rest marks silence in written music. It is part of the music's timing, rather than an instruction to abandon or finish the piece.

title: Songs & Singing
cardDescription: Voices, song sections, and the words we sing together.
description: Hum along in your imagination while solving simple clues about voices, song sections, and singing alone or together.
focus: This puzzle uses the vocabulary of singing without asking you to quote lyrics or identify a recording. Some answers name parts of a song; others describe a voice or a group of performers. The clues explain which meaning is intended when a word can have several uses.
solvingTip: Count the performers when a clue describes a group: one, two, or three can point to different short words. For song sections, look for whether the words change or a section returns. Those details are more useful than guessing from length alone.
words: Make musical sounds with the voice
A piece of music written to be sung
Section of a song whose words often change when it returns
Repeated song section often containing its main hook
A recurring line or phrase in a song
A sequence of pitches heard as a recognizable tune
Sing a tune with closed lips and no words
The sound a person produces when speaking or singing
A musical performance by one person
A musical performance by two people
A group or performance involving three musicians
Air taken in before singing a phrase
An open speech sound such as the sound of ah
Different musical pitches sounded together to support a tune
Singing the same notes together, rather than different harmony parts
Choral voice part traditionally below soprano and above tenor
Choral voice part traditionally below alto and above bass
High choral voice part traditionally above alto

answerNotes.VERSE: Verses often share a melody while changing their words. That contrasts with a chorus, which commonly returns with the same main words and tune.
answerNotes.REFRAIN: A refrain can be a recurring line or phrase. Chorus often names a larger recurring section, although everyday use of the terms can overlap.
answerNotes.UNISON: In unison, singers follow the same notes together. Harmony involves different pitches sounding together, which is why the clue contrasts the two ideas.
answerNotes.DUET: A duet is written or performed for two participants. Trio refers to three, while solo refers to one; the number in the clue selects the word.
answerNotes.ALTO: Alto names a voice part in a common choral arrangement. The clue describes its position relative to soprano and tenor rather than assigning it to a particular person.
answerNotes.HUM: Humming carries a melody without sung words, usually with the lips closed. A clue that mentions closed lips points to the action rather than to a song section.

title: Rhythm & Dance
cardDescription: Familiar dances and the musical pulse that keeps them moving.
description: Think of familiar dance steps and a steady musical pulse as you solve a gentle crossword about rhythm and social dancing.
focus: The answers mix familiar dance names with words for timing and movement. The puzzle does not require you to hear an audio clip or perform a step. Country, time signature, or a partial name gives an extra clue when several dances might otherwise seem possible.
solvingTip: A dance name and a timing word can have the same number of letters. Notice whether the clue describes a particular dance, its speed, or a single movement. Start with a familiar name, then use crossings to fill the shorter timing terms.
words: Ballroom dance usually counted in groups of three beats

The person with whom someone dances as a pair
The surface on which dancers take their steps
Guide a partner's movement in a paired dance

answerNotes.WALTZ: The familiar ballroom waltz is counted in three beats to a measure. The clue uses the usual dance pattern, not a claim that every composition called a waltz follows the same rules.
answerNotes.TEMPO: Tempo is musical speed. Beat is the pulse, and rhythm is the pattern of sounds and silences; these related ideas are not interchangeable.
answerNotes.TWIST: The clue asks for the dance associated with Chubby Checker's early-1960s recordings. It does not ask for the singer's name or any lyrics.
answerNotes.FOXTROT: Foxtrot is a smooth ballroom dance. The partial-name clue supplies 'trot' to make a longer answer approachable even if you have never learned the steps.
answerNotes.TAP: Tap dancing uses the sound of taps on the shoes as part of its rhythm. The short answer names the dance style, not a hand movement.
answerNotes.LEAD: Lead is used here as a verb meaning to guide a partner. Its pronunciation and meaning differ from the metal spelled the same way.

title: Meet the Orchestra
cardDescription: Strings, brass, woodwinds, and the parts that help them sound.
description: Meet familiar orchestral instruments through direct clues about their shapes, sounds, and the ways musicians play them.
focus: This puzzle names instruments and a few of their playing parts. Clues distinguish an instrument from the bow, reed, or other part used with it. Common instrument names are used instead of composers, concert dates, or specialist repertoire.
solvingTip: Look for how the sound is made. A clue about plucked strings points somewhere different from one about a reed or a brass bell. A partial name such as 'double ___' can provide a foothold among the longer instrument names.
words: Small four-string orchestral instrument usually held under the chin
Bowed string instrument larger than a violin and tuned a fifth lower
Bowed string instrument played upright between the seated musician's knees
Large instrument with many strings that are usually plucked
Woodwind instrument commonly held sideways and played without a reed
Slender orchestral woodwind played with a double reed
Large, low-pitched woodwind played with a double reed
Woodwind with a single reed attached to its mouthpiece
High brass instrument often played with three valves

Large, low-pitched brass instrument with a broad bell

Orchestral kettledrums whose pitch can be adjusted
Round metal percussion disc struck or clashed to make sound

Double ___: the large, low-pitched orchestral string instrument
Hair-strung stick drawn across a violin's strings
Thin vibrating blade used in instruments such as a clarinet

answerNotes.VIOLA: The viola resembles a violin but is larger and tuned lower. The size and tuning details help distinguish two similar-looking bowed instruments.
answerNotes.OBOE: An oboe uses a double reed, made from two blades vibrating against each other. A clarinet uses a single reed against a mouthpiece.
answerNotes.HARP: A harp's strings are usually plucked directly. That separates it from bowed strings such as the violin or cello, even though all belong to the broad string family.
answerNotes.TROMBONE: The familiar slide trombone changes the length of its tubing with a sliding section. Valve trombones also exist, so the clue describes the common slide form rather than every trombone.
answerNotes.BASS: Double bass is the name of a large orchestral string instrument. Bass can also describe a low voice or register, but the partial instrument name fixes the intended meaning.
answerNotes.REED: Reed names the vibrating blade rather than the whole instrument. Clarinet and oboe clues specify how the reed is arranged, helping you separate the part from the instrument.
